methodology/.html:
The thesis

One number. One mechanism.

AI assistants don’t recommend the closest business, the prettiest website, or whoever paid the most. They recommend a business they can retrieve and recognize as real: one that many independent, trustworthy sources describe the same way.

Because retrieval is the gate everything else passes through, the single heaviest signal is whether you appear in the results an AI model pulls from when it answers. Everything else either earns that retrievability or refines what the AI says once you’re in.

Retrievability isn’t one ranking factor among many. It’s the precondition for all of them.

The weights

How much each signal weighs.

Eight signals, identical for every business, ordered by how much each one moves an AI recommendation. The single heaviest is whether you can be retrieved at all.

Retrievability and the attestation that earns it are the retrieval tier — together 46% of the score. Nearly half.

It measures how likely AI engines are to recommend a business, and how accurately. The same method scores every business on the registry. Every business is scored the same way, and nobody can pay for a better score. Fair starts at 45, good at 65.

Retrieval tier 26%Retrieval groundingWhether you appear in the ranked results AI retrieves and cites: AI-Overview citations, organic top-10 for your money queries, and the Bing index ChatGPT leans on. 20%Off-property attestationVolume and consistency of what others say about you: YouTube mentions, branded web mentions, third-party “best-of” lists. The cause of retrievability. 14%AI visibilityWhether ChatGPT, Gemini, Perplexity, and AI Overviews name you, and whether they name you for the right service. 12%Reviews & responseThe star average is only one input. We also read volume, velocity, the specificity of review language, and response cadence. Specific reviews are what AI quotes verbatim. 8%Backlink & citation authorityDomain authority and editorial quality of the sources that attest to you. 8%Google Business ProfileRequired and recommended fields; update cadence. The listing AI pulls from first. 7%Speed & mobileCore Web Vitals at the 75th percentile, on a real phone. 5%Content freshness & schemaCrawl recency, intent alignment, valid JSON-LD, canonicals.

Methods referenced

We didn’t invent the maths.

Every part of the score is a named, published method, borrowed from information retrieval, index construction, and game theory, and each one is cited.

Fig. 8 — Methods composing the AI Score · n = 10 · 3 stages · full citations

Reading a business page

What the marks on a business page mean

Every fact on a business page carries one of three marks, and every mark points to a reference at the end of that page.

Confirmedsolid circle
From a known source: the business's website, its Google Business Profile, review sites like Yelp, Healthgrades and RealSelf, a licensing board, or measured by Local AI Registry.
Visitor submittedhollow circle
Added or corrected by a person, with the date and how they know, like a phone call or a visit.
AI guesshollow triangle
What AI engines like ChatGPT, Gemini and Perplexity are saying right now. Nobody has confirmed it.

Each row is marked Confirmed, Visitor submitted or AI guess, with where it came from. Each reference names the fact, the source, what kind of source it is, and the date it was checked, with a link and an archived copy so anyone can verify it. Visitor references are dated firsthand accounts. AI guesses record what an AI engine said on that date, not what is true.

How AI reads a business

How AI decides what to tell you about a med spa

When you ask ChatGPT, Gemini or Google for a med spa, the AI doesn't visit each business. It reads what's already written about it: the business's website, its Google Business Profile, review sites like Yelp and RealSelf, news stories, licensing boards and directories like ours. Then it repeats what those sources agree on.

That's why AI gets small facts wrong. If Yelp says a place is open Mondays and the website says it isn't, the AI has to pick one. Each business page on the registry lists the answers that disagree with what we've confirmed.

The more sources agree, and the more specific they are, the more confidently AI recommends a business. A review that says "the nurse did half a syringe in my lips and it looks natural" is far more useful to an AI than one that says "great place."

How AI decides what to tell you about an eye surgery practice

When you ask ChatGPT, Gemini or Google for an eye surgeon, the AI doesn't visit the practice. It reads what's already written about it: the practice's website, its Google Business Profile, review sites like Healthgrades and Yelp, your state's medical and optometry boards, news stories and directories like ours. Then it repeats what those sources agree on.

That's why AI gets small facts wrong. If one site says a surgeon still operates there and the practice's own website doesn't list them, the AI has to pick one. Each business page on the registry lists the answers that disagree with what we've confirmed.

The more sources agree, and the more specific they are, the more confidently AI recommends a practice. A review that says "my surgeon did my cataract surgery on a Tuesday and I was driving by Friday" is far more useful to an AI than one that says "great doctor."

How AI decides what to tell you about a local business

When you ask ChatGPT, Gemini or Google about a local business, the AI doesn't visit it. It reads what's already written about it: the business's website, its Google Business Profile, review sites, news stories and directories like ours. Then it repeats what those sources agree on.

That's why AI gets small facts wrong. If Yelp says a place is open Mondays and the website says it isn't, the AI has to pick one. Each business page on the registry lists the answers that disagree with what we've confirmed.

The more sources agree, and the more specific they are, the more confidently AI recommends a business. A review that names who helped and what they did tells an AI far more than one that says "great place."

Before you choose

How to choose a med spa, with or without AI

A few checks take ten minutes and matter more than any rating. This is general information, not medical advice.

  1. 01Look up every injector. Doctors are listed by your state's medical board, and nurses and nurse practitioners by its nursing board. Both lookups are free.
  2. 02Ask who does the injections, and check that person's license.
  3. 03Ask for the price per unit of Botox and per syringe of filler, not per area.
  4. 04Read reviews that name a provider and a treatment. Vague praise is easy to fake.
  5. 05Check that the hours and phone number match on Google and the website. Mismatches are how people end up at a locked door.
  6. 06Ask whether they dissolve filler and when they would tell you not to add more.

How to choose an eye surgery practice, with or without AI

A few checks take ten minutes and matter more than any rating. This is general information, not medical advice.

  1. 01Look up the surgeon who'll operate on you. Your state's medical board lists every ophthalmologist, and its optometry board lists the optometrists who do your exams and follow-ups. Both lookups are free.
  2. 02Ask who does the surgery itself and who sees you before and after it. At many practices those are different people.
  3. 03Ask which laser or lens they use for your procedure, and why it suits your eyes.
  4. 04Ask what the consult covers, how long it takes, and whether your eyes will be dilated so you need a ride home.
  5. 05Ask what your insurance pays for and what it leaves you to pay. Cataract surgery is often covered and LASIK usually is not.
  6. 06Read reviews that name a surgeon and a procedure. Vague praise is easy to fake.

How to choose a local business, with or without AI

A few checks take ten minutes and tell you more than any rating.

  1. 01Check that the hours and phone number match on Google and the business's own website. Mismatches are how people end up at a locked door.
  2. 02Read reviews that name a person and what they did. Vague praise is easy to fake.
  3. 03Look for recent reviews and recent posts. A page nobody has touched in a year may not match the business today.
  4. 04Ask for the price before you go, and ask what it includes.
  5. 05Where the work needs a license, ask whose license it is and look it up with your state.

Find out what AI says about you.

And it’s free.

How to read this report

The view from above — and how it's written

Most research on AI search reports one study at a time. This report does the opposite. It gathers every bucket of evidence we could find on how local businesses get recommended by AI, lays them on one table, and steps back until the whole picture resolves. From that altitude, the disconnected facts collapse into a single conclusion and four currents that run beneath all of them.

Because the goal is to be useful to a business owner and defensible to a skeptic, every section is written twice. In Plain Terms states the point in language anyone can act on. The Proof then establishes it rigorously — naming the specific researcher, study, court record, or dataset behind each claim, with the chart that shows it.

How every claim is labelled

  • CITED A figure from a named, linkable source. Real or omitted — never invented.
  • ANALYSIS Our own conclusion from reading the sources together.
  • PROJECTION A forward inference from a measured trend. Flagged, never disguised as data.

I · The Convergence — eleven streams, one substrate

In Plain Terms

We pulled together every kind of evidence we could find about how AI decides which local businesses to recommend — what shoppers do, what the data shows, what Google's own people and documents say, what scientists have proven about how these systems retrieve information, and what the law now requires. They come from totally different places and were never meant to be read together. But when you put them side by side, they all say the same thing: AI doesn't recommend a website, a profile, or whoever is closest. It recommends a business it can recognize as real — one that many trustworthy sources independently describe the same way. Being that recognizable, verifiable business is the whole game.

The Proof

The diagram below places eleven independent research streams around a single center. Each was produced by different people, with different methods, for different reasons. Read individually they are a pile of disconnected facts. Read together they converge — every one of them describes, from its own angle, the same underlying object: the verifiable entity.

Eleven instruments, eleven methods, one reading: AI local visibility is won as a verifiable entity, attested consistently across independent sources.

That single substrate is the bird's-eye finding. Everything that follows — the four currents — is simply what this convergence does to a local business, and the one thing the whole landscape is still missing.

II · Current One — the battlefield left your property

It's no longer about what you publish

In Plain Terms

For twenty years, "doing your SEO" meant working on things you owned: your website, your pages, your Google profile. That era is ending. The things that now make AI recommend you mostly live off your own property — what other people say about you on YouTube, in reviews, in community threads, in local round-ups. You've gone from building your storefront to earning a reputation you don't fully control. The job is no longer to publish more about yourself; it's to be talked about, consistently, by others.

The Proof

Glenn Allsopp's Ahrefs analysis of 75,000 brands ranked every candidate signal by how strongly it correlates with AI visibility. The signals describing what others say about you — YouTube mentions (0.737), branded web mentions (0.66–0.71) — sit at the top. The signals describing what you publish about yourself — your domain rating (0.266), the backlinks you build (0.218), the pages you publish (0.194) — sit at the bottom.² The gap is not subtle.

Figure II · Off-property signals win. Ahrefs, 75,000 brands (Glenn Allsopp), 2026.

The mechanism, disclosed in Judge Amit Mehta's November 2025 ruling in U.S. v. Google, explains why. Google grounds its Gemini answers through a retriever called FastSearch, built on a deep-learning model, RankEmbed, that matches queries to documents semantically rather than by counting links.¹⁷ Google's own VP of Search, Robby Stein, describes the front end as "query fan-out" — the model issues dozens of background searches and synthesizes what it retrieves.¹² Neither process rewards a business for publishing more pages about itself; both reward a business that the wider web independently corroborates. ANALYSIS The practical relocation is total: the battlefield moved from your domain to the ecosystem's consensus about you.

III · Current Two — specificity is rewarded at every layer

Generic loses; specific wins — everywhere

In Plain Terms

The single most repeated pattern across all the evidence is this: the more specific you are, the more AI rewards you — and it shows up at every level. Specific questions get AI answers more often than vague searches. First-hand, specific content beats generic listicles. A review that names exactly what you did ("great with anxious dogs") is worth more than a bare five stars. And a business known for one clear thing beats one that claims to do everything. Being known for the right thing isn't a tagline — it's the rule the whole system runs on.

The Proof

The same generic-to-specific gradient appears independently at four layers. At the query layer, Ahrefs' study of 146 million SERPs shows single-word searches trigger an AI Overview 9.5% of the time, while full question-style queries trigger 57.9%.³ At the content layer, Google's own Search Central guidance explicitly rewards "non-commodity content" and first-hand experience over generic aggregation.¹⁰ At the review layer, AI answers quote the specific language of reviews verbatim — the named service, not the star count. At the entity layer, the retrieval-science consensus (LUKE-style entity grounding) favors precisely-described, unambiguous entities.³⁰

Figure III · The specificity ladder. Query: Ahrefs. Content: Google. Review/entity: platform mechanics & LAIR analysis.

This is the academic and mechanical basis for Local AI Registry's founding principle — alignment, not coverage. ANALYSIS A business fails in AI not by being invisible but by being known for the wrong, generic thing. The corrective is specificity, applied deliberately at all four layers at once.

IV · Current Three — four clocks, one transition window

Four unrelated timers strike at once

In Plain Terms

Four completely separate things are all changing at the same moment — roughly 2026 into 2027. How many people use AI for local search. How open AI is to recommending smaller businesses. How people phrase their searches. And when the new AI transparency laws kick in. None of these has anything to do with the others — which is exactly why their lining up matters. When four unrelated clocks all strike the same hour, that's not coincidence; it's a transition. The businesses that move during the window get an advantage the latecomers won't.

The Proof

Four independently-measured trends converge on the same window. Adoption: BrightLocal records consumer use of AI for local discovery rising from 6% to 45% across 2025–26.¹ The citation window: Ahrefs finds the share of AI-Overview citations drawn from the organic top ten fell from ~76% to ~38%, widening the pool to the long tail — a window the retrieval-bias literature predicts will re-narrow.⁴,²⁵ The exposure runway: as phrasing turns conversational, local AI-trigger rates climb off their 7.9% floor toward the 57.9% question rate.³ Regulation: the EU AI Act's Article 50 transparency duties take effect 2 August 2026.³⁸

The convergence itself is the argument. ANALYSIS Any one trend could be dismissed as noise; four unrelated research streams agreeing on a transition date is a structural signal that the ground is shifting now, and that early, consistent action dominates a wait-and-see posture.

V · Current Four — the accountability vacuum

The Keystone · No one can tell you what the AI says

In Plain Terms

Here's the strangest part. Everything above says your AI reputation now matters enormously — but nobody can actually tell you what it is. Ask the same question twice and the AI gives different answers. The platforms don't report which businesses they recommend or why. There's no record that follows you across ChatGPT, Gemini, and Google. And the law polices AI that lies to customers, not AI that's wrong about you. So the one thing that now decides whether customers find you is the one thing no one is keeping score of. That gap is the whole reason a registry needs to exist.

The Proof

Four properties you would expect of any system of record are absent across every major AI surface. Reproducibility: practitioners document that AI Overview results "aren't repeatable" run-to-run, and Google's own Search Console does not separate AI-driven clicks. Accuracy: Nelson Liu and Percy Liang (Stanford) found only 51.5% of generated sentences are fully supported by their citations, and the Tow Center at Columbia found leading AI search tools wrong on more than 60% of queries.³²,³⁴ Cross-platform record: none exists. Regulatory scope: the FTC and EU AI Act target deception of consumers, not accuracy about third-party businesses.³⁵,³⁸

51.5%of generated sentences are fully supported by their citations. CITED: N. F. Liu, T. Zhang, P. Liang (Stanford), Evaluating Verifiability in Generative Search Engines. More than 60%of queries: leading AI search tools wrong. CITED: Tow Center at Columbia, AI Search Has a Citation Problem.

Figure V · The accountability vacuum. LAIR analysis of platform reporting, reproducibility & regulatory scope, 2026.

This is the keystone the other three currents rest on. ANALYSIS The entire body of evidence converges on "be a verifiable entity," moving fast, on a closing clock — while no neutral party measures whether you are one, reproducibly, across platforms, over time. That negative space, visible only when all eleven streams are held in one frame, is not a gap in the research. It is a description of an institution that does not yet exist.

VI · The Instrument — what the vacuum implies

If the evidence converges on a substrate no one is measuring, the implied object is not a tactic or a tool — it is an institution: an independent, reproducible record of what AI says about local businesses, and whether they are known for the right things.

That is the function Local AI Registry performs. It scores independent local businesses across ChatGPT, Gemini, Perplexity, and Google AI Overviews; it measures not just whether a business is named but whether it is named for the right service — the alignment this report shows the whole system rewards; and it does so repeatedly, across platforms, over time, which is exactly the reproducibility the landscape lacks. The registry is not a product appended to the research. It is the instrument the convergence implies.

From reading to record

A reader can act on the four currents today: move the work off-property, apply specificity at every layer, act within the window, and treat verifiability as a conversion advantage. But to know where you stand — what you're named for, what you're invisible for, where the reputation and the marketing diverge — requires the instrument. That is what the next page offers.

VII · The evidence layer — seven findings underneath

Seven findings underneath the view

The bird's-eye view is built on a deeper layer of cross-source findings — each one a conclusion drawn by overlaying two or three datasets that none of them states alone. They are summarized here as the supporting evidence beneath the four currents; each is documented at length in companion analysis.

The seven triangulated findings beneath the convergence

  • 01 · The Broken Scoreboard. The canonical local-pack model and AI visibility are nearly orthogonal. Built from: Ahrefs × Whitespark × antitrust.
  • 02 · The Exposure Runway. The 7.9% local AI rate is a countdown toward the 57.9% question rate. Built from: Ahrefs × BrightLocal.
  • 03 · Re-Centralization. Proximity's death plus prominence bias tilts AI toward incumbents. Built from: Local Falcon × retrieval-bias research.
  • 04 · The Closing Window. A temporary long-tail citation opening that bias predicts will re-narrow. Built from: Ahrefs × field experiment × academia.
  • 05 · Reviews Are the Keystone. The only lever that is ranking signal, citation source, safeguard & legal moat at once. Built from: Whitespark × mechanism × Liu × FTC.
  • 06 · The Verification Dividend. The fact-check, not the recommendation, is where the funnel breaks. Built from: BrightLocal × Tow Center.
  • 07 · Two Disjoint Games. ChatGPT-via-Bing visibility is the underpriced channel. Built from: Seer × Ahrefs × Sensor Tower.

Each finding is graded ANALYSIS — a strong hypothesis from real, cited inputs, not a measured fact. Several become measurable original statistics when cross-checked against the live index; those measurements will be published when complete.

Methodology & limitations

How this report was built

This is a work of synthesis at altitude: eleven independent evidence streams, read together to surface the conclusions that only their overlap reveals. Every input is a real, cited figure from a named source; the convergence and the four currents are our own ANALYSIS; forward inferences are marked PROJECTION. We hold a strict "real or omitted" rule — no quote, statistic, study, court finding, or researcher is invented, and unverifiable figures (such as a widely-shared "797,444 impressions, 7 clicks" anecdote) are excluded rather than repeated.

What this method can and cannot claim

Convergence is strong evidence, not proof of mechanism. Many independent sources agreeing on a substrate is a powerful signal, but several inputs are correlational and inherit that limit. Projections are reasoned, not certain — the transition window and the runway are extrapolations from measured trends, flagged as such. The local-AI research gap is real: little peer-reviewed work studies local-business inclusion in AI answers directly, so local conclusions are careful inferences from adjacent retrieval, bias, and entity-grounding research. Vendor incentive exists in some sources; figures were cross-checked where possible. The accountability vacuum is, by definition, where measurement is thinnest — which is precisely the gap the registry is built to close, and why proprietary figures are shown as forthcoming rather than asserted.

Reference numbers are shared across the Local AI Visibility Series for cross-referencing; gaps indicate sources cited in companion papers.

Section 01

Introduction

Local AI Registry is a product of Blind LLC (“we,” “our,” or “us”). When we say “the Services,” we mean our website at localairegistry.com, the owner dashboards it hosts, the public business profile pages we generate, the review-collection and photo-upload tools we host on your behalf, and the integrations that connect those tools to Google and the other platforms listed below.

By using the Services, you accept the practices described in this policy. If you do not agree, please do not use the Services. We’ll always tell you when this document materially changes (see Section 14).

Section 02

Information we collect

Information you give us directly

When you create an account, claim a business, or buy a plan, you provide your name, email address, phone number, business name and address, the services your business offers, and the keywords you want us to track. If you pay for a plan, your card details go directly to our payment processor — we never store or see full card numbers, CVV codes, or bank details.

Information from the public web and our partners

For every business we surface on the public site, we collect information from Google Maps, public review platforms, business websites we scrape with permission, and SEO data providers (DataForSEO and others listed in Section 7). This includes hours, categories, photos, opening times, popular times, organic keyword rankings, backlinks, and reviews. We compute a Digital Score from these signals.

Information from connected accounts

When you authorize a paid plan that includes the Google Business Profile integration, we receive access tokens that let us read and (with your approval) write to your listing on your behalf. See Section 4 for exactly what we do with that access, and how to revoke it at any time.

Information collected automatically

When you visit the public site or your dashboard, we record limited usage information: your IP address (used briefly for spam protection and rate limiting), browser and device type, the pages you view, and how you arrived. We use this to keep the site fast, fix bugs, and protect against abuse.

We log a salted SHA-256 hash of (IP + 30-minute time bucket) on public profile pageviews so business owners can see how many distinct visitors viewed their profile this week without us storing the raw IP. After the bucket window expires, the hash cannot be reversed.

Customers your business sends to us

If you use our review collection or photo upload tools, your customers may give us their name, rating, written feedback, and photos via your branded link. We process this on your behalf as your service provider; you remain the controller of that data. We do not contact those customers for any reason other than the flow they entered.

Section 03

How we use your information

We use the information described in Section 2 to:

  • Provide, operate, secure, and improve the Services.
  • Compute Digital Scores and editorial summaries for every business listed on the public site.
  • Deliver the SEO modules you have purchased — including drafting Google Business Profile posts, replying to reviews, building citations, and producing monthly reports.
  • Process payments, manage subscriptions, and prevent fraud.
  • Send transactional messages: phone verification codes, approval requests, billing receipts, weekly progress digests, and monthly reports.
  • Respond to support requests and dispute resolution.
  • Comply with legal obligations and enforce our Terms of Service.

We do not sell your personal information. We do not share it for cross-context behavioral advertising. We do not buy advertising profiles to target you.

Section 04

Google API Services data

Local AI Registry accesses your Google account data only with your explicit OAuth authorization and only for the purposes you sign up for. Local AI Registry’s use and transfer of information received from Google APIs to any other app will adhere to the Google API Services User Data Policy, including the Limited Use requirements.

Scopes we may request

Depending on the modules you purchase, we request access to the following Google services:

Sign in with Google
Basic profile (name, email, profile photo) so you can log in to Local AI Registry with your Google account.
Google Business Profile
Read your business listing details, posts, photos, reviews, and Q&A. Write new posts, photos, and review replies on your behalf when you approve them (or pre-approve them via Auto-Approve in Settings).

How we use Google data

Google account information is used solely to identify you when you sign in. Google Business Profile data is used to populate your owner dashboard, surface what needs attention, draft content for your approval, and publish that content to your listing after you (or your designated approver) approve it. We do not use Google data to train generalized AI/ML models, and we do not transfer Google data to third parties except the sub-processors strictly necessary to operate the Services (Section 7).

How to revoke access

You can revoke our access to your Google account at any time at myaccount.google.com/permissions. When you revoke access, any pending automated actions on your Google Business Profile are cancelled within minutes. The associated tokens are deleted from our systems within 24 hours.

Section 05

AI-generated content

Local AI Registry uses large language models (OpenAI and Google Gemini, principally) to draft Google Business Profile posts, review replies, FAQ answers, monthly report narratives, and content suggestions. These drafts are generated against your business’s data, your selected brand voice, and your written brand rules.

Every AI-generated artifact that publishes to a public platform passes through an approval gate by default. You can pre-approve specific content types under Settings → Auto-Approve, in which case those drafts ship without per-item review — you remain fully responsible for the published output. We log every draft, every approval, and every publish so you can audit the chain end-to-end from your dashboard.

AI providers may briefly cache prompts and responses for safety and abuse-monitoring purposes per their published policies. We do not authorize providers to use your data for model training, and we use API tiers that contractually prohibit such use where available.

Section 06

Cookies and similar technologies

Local AI Registry uses a small number of essential cookies: a session cookie when you log in, a CSRF protection cookie, and a preference cookie for any dashboard layout choices you make.

We also use two privacy-respecting analytics tools to understand how the site is used: Google Analytics and Microsoft Clarity. They tell us which pages people visit, how they arrive, and where the site is slow or confusing. Microsoft Clarity records anonymized session activity — clicks, scrolls, and page navigation — so we can find and fix bugs and rough edges. We use this only to measure and improve the Services. We do not use advertising cookies, we do not sell your information, and we do not track you across other sites for advertising (see Section 3).

Where we use a third party to deliver part of the Services (a hosted Stripe Checkout page, for example), that third party may set its own cookies on its own domain; their cookie policies govern that use.

Section 07

Third-party processors

We rely on the sub-processors below to operate the Services. Each one receives only the data needed for its specific function, under a data-processing agreement that restricts re-use. You can request a current list at any time by contacting us.

Stripe
Payment processing, subscription billing, customer portal. We send Stripe your email, business name, and the modules you bought.
Twilio
Phone-number verification (SMS OTP) and outbound transactional SMS. We send Twilio your phone number and the message to deliver.
Resend
Transactional email (verification, approval requests, weekly digests, monthly reports). We send Resend recipient email addresses and message contents.
Google (Cloud, Places, Maps, PageSpeed, Business Profile)
Sign-in, location autocomplete, map rendering, site performance scoring, GBP read and write. Data flows are scoped per Section 4.
DataForSEO
Keyword ranking data, SERP screenshots, organic traffic estimates, backlink data, review ingestion, business listing data. We send DataForSEO public business identifiers (website, name, address, GBP placeId) and target keywords.
BrightLocal
Citation campaign management for paid customers on the Off-Page module. We send BrightLocal the business NAP (name, address, phone) and category data.
OpenAI
AI-generated content drafting (posts, replies, summaries, reports). We send OpenAI sanitized prompts containing business context, brand voice notes, and content goals. We use API tiers that prohibit training use of submitted data.
Google Gemini
AI-generated content drafting and AI visibility checks. Same handling as OpenAI.
SerpZilla / SerpClix / Adsy / RedPress
Off-page module vendors used only for customers actively enrolled in those modules — backlinks, CTR campaigns, press release distribution.
DigitalOcean
Application hosting, managed Postgres, object storage (DO Spaces) for photos and report PDFs.
Cloudflare
CDN, DDoS protection, bot mitigation in front of public routes.
Sentry
Error monitoring. Sentry may capture stack traces and request metadata when our application encounters an error. We scrub personally identifying parameters before sending.

No mobile information will be shared with third parties or affiliates for marketing or promotional purposes. Information sharing to subcontractors in support services, such as customer service, is permitted. All other use case categories exclude text messaging originator opt-in data and consent; this information will not be shared with any third parties.

Section 08

When we disclose your information

We disclose information only in these specific circumstances:

  • To deliver the Services. The sub-processors in Section 7 receive what they need to do their job and nothing more.
  • With your direction. If you connect Google, or instruct us to publish content, we transmit the corresponding data to those platforms on your behalf.
  • To comply with law. We may disclose information when required by a valid subpoena, court order, or government request. We push back where the request is overbroad and notify you where we are legally permitted to do so.
  • To protect rights and safety. Where necessary to investigate fraud, security incidents, or violations of our Terms of Service.
  • Business transfer. If Blind LLC is acquired or merged, customer data transfers to the acquirer under the same protections.

Section 09

Data retention

We keep account data for as long as your account is active, plus a short tail to handle disputes, support, and legal obligations. Specifically:

  • Account profile and business data: kept while the account is active; deleted within 30 days of account closure (or sooner on request).
  • OAuth tokens (Google): deleted within 24 hours of revocation or account closure.
  • Pageview hashes (Section 2): raw IP is never persisted; the salted hash is kept for 13 months for week-over-week trend reporting, then purged.
  • Billing records: retained for 7 years to meet tax and accounting obligations.
  • Application logs: 30 days, then purged.
  • Public business profile pages we generate from the public web persist as long as the underlying business is operational. Owners can flag inaccurate data or request removal — see Section 11.

Section 10

Data security

We protect data with industry-standard controls: TLS in transit, AES-256 at rest in managed Postgres and object storage, encrypted secrets, least-privilege access management, structured access logs, and continuous error monitoring. OAuth tokens are stored encrypted with separate key material. Production database access is restricted to a small set of authorized engineers and audited.

No system is impenetrable, so we maintain an incident-response plan and will notify affected users without undue delay if a breach occurs that materially affects their data.

Section 11

Your rights and choices

You can:

  • Access the personal information we hold about you by emailing the address in Section 15.
  • Correct inaccurate information directly in your dashboard, or by writing to us.
  • Delete your account and associated personal information at any time from Settings → Account, or by writing to us.

If you are in the United Kingdom or another jurisdiction with similar laws (GDPR, UK GDPR), you additionally have the right to lodge a complaint with your local supervisory authority. If you are a California resident, you have rights under the CCPA / CPRA including the right to know what we collect, the right to delete, the right to correct, and the right not to be discriminated against for exercising your rights. We honor all of these rights regardless of your jurisdiction.

International transfers

If you are accessing the Services from outside the United States (including the United Kingdom), your information will be transferred to and processed in the United States. We rely on Standard Contractual Clauses or equivalent mechanisms with our sub-processors where required.

Section 13

Children

The Services are intended for businesses and adults. We do not knowingly collect personal information from anyone under 13 (or under 16 in jurisdictions that apply a higher age). If we learn that we have inadvertently collected such information, we will delete it promptly.

Changes to this policy

research/how-often-ai-recommends-your-bu.title: How Often AI Recommends Your Business | Local AI Registry
research/how-often-ai-recommends-your-bu.desc: Local AI Registry reviews 14 sources: ask AI the same thing twice and Gemini’s sources overlap by only 0.46. How to measure how often AI recommends you.
research/how-often-ai-recommends-your-bu.html:
Key findings

  1. In research reviewed by Local AI Registry, the same query run twice shared 0.78 of its sources on Google Search, 0.66 on Google AI Overviews and 0.46 on Gemini (Grossman et al., SIGIR 2026).
  2. In a preprint census of cafés, restaurants and bars in Bali reviewed by Local AI Registry, the overlap between repeated runs of the same query ranged from 0.45 for Gemini to 0.22 for Claude.
  3. When ChatGPT was asked the same local question twice, a median of 39 minutes apart, a median of 29% of the businesses named in either answer were named in both, according to 8ight.AI data reviewed by Local AI Registry.
  4. Only 10.8% of doctors named by an AI model without web search matched a real clinician in the queried city, versus 63.9% with web search on, in a preprint audit of the 100 largest US metro areas reviewed by Local AI Registry.
  5. Wording changes who AI recommends: 74.7% of the people recommended for “an oculoplastic surgeon” were oculoplastic specialists, versus 46.6% for “a doctor who does eyelid lifts,” in a peer-reviewed study reviewed by Local AI Registry.
  6. ChatGPT declined to recommend an orthopedic surgeon in 52.8% of 40,500 persona-based requests, and stated income, insurance status and location were the strongest predictors of a recommendation, according to research reviewed by Local AI Registry.
  7. Only 3.5% of the businesses ChatGPT named in localized searches appeared at every point tested across a town, according to BrightLocal’s 2026 analysis reviewed by Local AI Registry.
  8. In the Bali census reviewed by Local AI Registry, 85.6% of venues were never recommended by any of the four AI systems, and being named was associated with documentation such as a website, more reviews, listed prices and mentions elsewhere on the web.
  9. Local AI Registry calculated that a business named in 40% of AI answers has a 95% confidence interval of roughly 17% to 69% after 10 answers and 31% to 50% after 100, so one answer cannot measure AI visibility.

What is AI visibility, and why can’t one answer measure it?

Visibility in AI-generated local recommendations is best measured as how often a business is named under stated conditions. A single answer is a genuine observation, but on its own it cannot reliably estimate that frequency.

Consumers are adopting generative assistants for local decisions at speed. In BrightLocal’s 2026 survey of 1,002 US consumers, 45% reported using ChatGPT or another generative AI tool to find local businesses, up from 6% a year earlier.1 As the behavior has spread, so has an informal method of judging it. An owner, marketer or analyst asks an assistant for the best provider in a category and city, and reads the reply as a verdict on where a business stands.

That reading carries over an assumption from conventional search, where a page of results could reasonably be treated as a ranking. A generative assistant does not return a stored list. It composes an answer at the moment of the request, from whatever it retrieves and infers under that request’s particular conditions. The research reviewed here points to a different unit of analysis.

Terms used in this brief

AI visibility
How often, how prominently and how accurately a business is named in AI answers, measured as a rate across many answers to the same question.
Recommendation frequency
The share of AI answers that name a business under a stated set of systems, configurations, locations, phrasings and dates.
Answer engine optimization (AEO)
Making a business’s facts clear, consistent and machine-readable so AI systems include it accurately in their answers.
Generative engine optimization (GEO)
The academic term for optimizing content to be cited by generative AI search engines; used interchangeably with AEO.
Overlap (Jaccard similarity)
What two runs returned in both, divided by what they returned in either. 1 means identical results; 0 means nothing in common.
Confidence interval
The range that likely contains the true rate. A 95% interval only becomes narrow after many answers have been collected.
Web search (grounding)
When an AI assistant searches the web during a request instead of answering only from what its model learned in training.
Algorithm audit
A way to study a system that cannot be inspected directly, by querying it repeatedly and recording what it returns.
Preprint
A research paper shared publicly before peer review.

Does AI recommend the same businesses every time you ask?

No. When the same query was run twice, Gemini’s sources overlapped by only 0.46, and in a census of Bali venues, Claude’s repeated local recommendations overlapped by just 0.22.

Variation in search results is not new. In a 2015 measurement study of Google Search, Kliman-Silver and colleagues found that 18% to 34% of results for local queries changed with the searcher’s location, and that local queries were also the noisiest category when repeated from the same place at the same time.2 Generative systems add another layer of variability, because the answer is written rather than retrieved.

The clearest controlled comparison is a study presented at ACM SIGIR 2026 that examined Google Search, Google’s AI Overviews and Gemini on more than 11,000 real user queries.3 When the same query was run twice, the overlap between the sources each system drew on, measured by Jaccard similarity, was 0.78 for conventional Search, 0.66 for AI Overviews and 0.46 for Gemini. Minor edits to a query, such as expanding a contraction or adding a question mark, reduced the rank-weighted similarity of AI Overview sources by 29%, compared with 14% for conventional Search.

Audits of local recommendations show the same pattern in the businesses named. A pre-registered census of every café, restaurant and bar in two Bali submarkets, conducted by a company that sells AI-visibility tools, collected 2,208 answers from four assistants over seven days.4 Overlap between repeated runs of the same query ranged from 0.22 for Claude to 0.45 for Gemini. The study’s most consequential finding concerns time. When the queries were repeated two weeks later, overlap with the original answers (0.375) was comparable to overlap between reruns within the same period, and the author attributes most of the variation to sampling rather than drift.

The distinction matters for measurement. If answers drifted steadily, the most recent answer would be an imperfect but current reading. If answers instead scatter around a relatively stable underlying tendency, as this evidence suggests, the tendency is the quantity worth estimating. Each answer is one observation of it, and only an accumulation of observations can show how strong it is.

AEO takeaway

One AI answer is a snapshot, not a ranking.

What to do

Do not judge your AI visibility from one screenshot. Ask the same customer questions several times, on more than one assistant, and count how often your business is named.

How Local AI Registry does it

Local AI Registry’s AI visibility audit shows how a business appears in AI answers today, where answers are wrong, and what competitors are cited for.

What changes which business AI recommends?

Four conditions: the AI system and its settings, the place, the wording of the request, and time. With web search on, 63.9% of the doctors an AI model named matched a real clinician in the queried city, versus 10.8% with it off.

There is no single frequency. A business can be named often under some conditions and rarely under others. The literature identifies four sets of conditions that change the answer, and a credible measurement has to state which of them it holds fixed.

System and configuration. The assistant, the model behind it and whether it searches the web during the request all change the outcome. In an audit of provider recommendations across the 100 largest US metropolitan areas, Ibrahim and Zaki found that only 10.8% of doctors named by a proprietary model without web search matched a real clinician in the queried city; with search enabled, the same model reached 63.9%.5 Systems also draw on different evidence. For “near me” queries in the SIGIR study, the overlap between sources used by AI Overviews and Gemini was 0.07.3 Disagreement between platforms predates generative AI: Li and Hecht found that Google Maps ratings averaged about 0.7 stars higher than Yelp ratings for the same restaurants, and that the two platforms’ top-ten lists for a metropolitan area overlapped little.6

Place. Location operates at more than one scale. Between cities, Ibrahim and Zaki found that without search the share of real doctors named fell from 16.3% in the largest third of metropolitan areas to 9.5% in the smallest, a gradient that largely disappeared once search was enabled.5 Haupt and colleagues found ChatGPT more likely to recommend an orthopedic surgeon for prompts set in New York City and Chicago than in Phoenix and Houston.7 Within a single town, BrightLocal’s 2026 analysis of localized searches found that only 3.5% of the businesses ChatGPT named appeared at every point tested across the area.8 Location effects are not uniform, however. For a stratified sample of general queries, the SIGIR study found that moving AI Overview requests from Newark to Austin reduced source similarity by only 0.01 to 0.02 relative to repeated runs from the same place.3 How much place matters appears to depend on the system and the kind of question.

Wording and context. The words in a request, and what it reveals about the person asking, change who is named. In a peer-reviewed study of chatbot recommendations for oculoplastic surgeons in the 20 largest US cities, 74.7% of the individuals recommended in response to “an oculoplastic surgeon” were oculoplastic specialists, compared with 46.6% for “a doctor who does eyelid lifts.”9 Haupt and colleagues submitted 40,500 persona-based requests for orthopedic surgeons to ChatGPT. It declined to recommend anyone in 52.8% of responses, and stated income, insurance status and location were the strongest predictors of whether a recommendation was given.7 Research on brand recommendations points the same way: language models recommended luxury gifts disproportionately to people from high-income countries.10

Time. Repetition alone changes answers, as both the SIGIR study and the Bali census show, and it does so over short intervals. 8ight.AI’s 2026 study of local trades found that when ChatGPT was asked the same question twice, a median of 39 minutes apart, a median of 29% of the businesses named in either answer were named in both.11 Over longer periods the systems themselves change, as model versions, retrieval sources and defaults are updated, which is why studies such as Parikh’s describe their findings as a record of a single point in time.9

AEO takeaway

State the conditions, or the number means nothing.

What to do

When you check what AI says about your business, write down the assistant, whether it searched the web, the city, the exact wording and the date, and keep them the same when you check again.

How Local AI Registry does it

Local AI Registry keeps an owner-confirmed public record of each business, so assistants that search the web find the same verified facts every time they look.

What can AI visibility research prove, and what can’t it?

It can show how often, and under which conditions, a business is named. It cannot show why. Only 51.5% of sentences written by generative search engines were fully supported by their citations, and 38.3% of ChatGPT’s surgeon suggestions in one study were excluded on review.

Three limits shape what any measurement of AI visibility can claim.

The first is that being named and being named first appear to be different outcomes. In the Bali census, 85.6% of venues were never recommended by any of the four systems. Inclusion was associated with documentation, including having a website, more reviews, listed prices and mentions elsewhere on the web, while star rating was associated only with whether a venue was named first.4 These are associations from one hospitality market, reported by a vendor-funded study, but they caution against collapsing inclusion and order into a single rank.

The second is that the sources an assistant displays are imperfect evidence of what produced its answer. In a peer-reviewed audit of four generative search engines, Liu, Zhang and Liang found that only 51.5% of generated sentences were fully supported by their citations, and only 74.5% of citations supported the sentence to which they were attached.12 Citation patterns can indicate which sources are prominent in a category. They cannot establish cause.

The third is that a name in an answer is not necessarily a correct name. In the 2023 oculoplastic study, 38.3% of ChatGPT’s suggestions were excluded on review; across the three chatbots studied, the most common reasons were a provider practicing in a different city or not existing at all.9 In the orthopedic study, 44.6% of recommended surgeons in a coded subset were valid.7 Counting mentions without verifying them can overstate visibility, and in healthcare the cost of that error falls on patients as well as practices.

Underlying all three is a broader point: visibility is partly defined by the instrument that measures it. The foundational paper on generative engine optimization (GEO), the research term for what practitioners call answer engine optimization (AEO), measured visibility with explicitly defined impression metrics and reported that content changes raised it by up to 40% on its benchmark, with effects that varied by domain.13 Findings of this kind show that visibility in generative answers responds to content. They do not show that a particular change will produce recommendations, or customers, for a particular business.

AEO takeaway

Being named is not the same as being named correctly.

What to do

Check that AI answers that name you have the right city, services and details, and fix the sources AI reads when they do not.

How Local AI Registry does it

Owners claim their Local AI Registry record for free and confirm each fact, which gives AI a verified source for the business’s name, location and services.

How should a business measure how often AI recommends it?

Count across many answers under fixed conditions. A business named in 40% of answers has a 95% range of roughly 17% to 69% after 10 answers and 31% to 50% after 100.

If visibility is a frequency to be estimated, its measurement belongs to the tradition of the algorithm audit, which studies a system that cannot be inspected directly by querying it repeatedly and recording what it returns.14 Read together, the evidence above suggests five principles for applying that method to local recommendations.

Five principles for measuring AI visibility

  1. Report a rate, with its conditions. The core quantity is the share of answers that name a business under a stated set of systems, configurations, locations, phrasings and dates. A rate reported without its conditions cannot be compared with another.
  2. Collect enough answers to support the claim. One answer records only whether a business was named on that occasion; it cannot distinguish a business named in nine answers out of ten from one named in one out of ten. Under fixed conditions, a business observed in 40% of answers has a 95% confidence interval of roughly 17% to 69% after ten answers and 31% to 50% after one hundred.
  3. Separate inclusion from order. Whether a business is named and where it appears when named respond to different factors and should be reported separately.
  4. Verify what is counted. A mention should count only when the business exists, operates in the location asked about and offers the service requested.
  5. Distinguish noise from change. A shift between two periods is meaningful only when it exceeds the variation seen within a period under the same protocol, the test the Bali census applied.
AEO takeaway

Measure a rate, not a rank.

What to do

Track the share of answers that name your business, collect enough answers to trust it, and treat a change as real only when it is bigger than the normal variation between checks.

How Local AI Registry does it

Local AI Registry’s free AI Score gives a broader diagnostic of how findable and recommendable a business is to ChatGPT, Gemini, Claude and Perplexity. It is a diagnostic, not the recommendation-frequency measure described in this brief.

What does this mean for local businesses?

The evidence changes the question worth asking. Whether a given assistant recommends a given business has no stable answer. How often the business is named, by which systems, for which requests, in which places, and how that frequency is moving does. Seen this way, AI visibility is not unknowable. It is measurable in the way other probabilistic systems are measured: through repeated, documented observation, with uncertainty stated and causes claimed only where the evidence supports them.

For local businesses, and for healthcare providers in particular, that discipline separates a reaction to one answer from an understanding of a market position that AI assistants increasingly help to shape. No intervention studied to date guarantees a recommendation. The research does support a narrower and more useful conclusion: visibility in AI-generated local recommendations can be observed, compared and tracked, provided it is estimated from many observations and not inferred from a single answer.

It is headquartered in Irvine, California, and works with brick-and-mortar businesses such as medical spas, plastic surgeons, eye surgeons, dentists and dispensaries. Its local AEO services include:

  • Free business record. A public, owner-claimable record of what AI says about the business, with every fact confirmed by the owner.
  • AI visibility audit. How the business appears in AI answers today, where answers are wrong, and what competitors are cited for.
  • Google Business Profile management. Location-level hours, holiday hours, services and updates kept current.
  • Press releases and media. Earned coverage in the news sources AI cites most for local questions.
  • AEO content. Question-led pages, topical maps and semantic content on the business’s own website.
  • Technical AEO. LocalBusiness schema, llms.txt, readable pages and AI-readable media.
  • Listing consistency. Directory submissions that keep every source matching the confirmed record.

Frequently asked questions

Does ChatGPT recommend the same businesses every time?

No. AI assistants compose a new answer for every request. When ChatGPT was asked the same local question twice, a median of 39 minutes apart, a median of 29% of the businesses named in either answer were named in both, according to 8ight.AI data reviewed by Local AI Registry. In a census of Bali venues, repeated runs of the same query overlapped by 0.22 for Claude and 0.45 for Gemini.

How do I know if AI recommends my business?

Ask the same customer questions many times, under the same conditions, and count the share of answers that name your business. One answer only shows whether you were named that one time. Local AI Registry’s free business record and AI visibility audit show what ChatGPT, Gemini, Claude and Perplexity say about a business today.

How many AI answers do I need to measure my AI visibility?

More than one, and usually many. Local AI Registry calculated that a business named in 40% of answers has a 95% confidence interval of roughly 17% to 69% after 10 answers and 31% to 50% after 100 answers, assuming the conditions stay the same.

Why does AI recommend different businesses in different places?

Place changes the answer. Without web search, the share of real doctors an AI model named fell from 16.3% in the largest third of US metro areas to 9.5% in the smallest (Ibrahim and Zaki, 2026, preprint). Within one town, BrightLocal found that only 3.5% of the businesses ChatGPT named appeared at every point tested.

Does web search change which businesses AI recommends?

Yes. In an audit of the 100 largest US metro areas, only 10.8% of doctors named by an AI model without web search matched a real clinician in the queried city; with web search on, the same model reached 63.9% (Ibrahim and Zaki, 2026, preprint).

Does the wording of a question change who AI recommends?

Yes. In a peer-reviewed study of chatbot recommendations in the 20 largest US cities, 74.7% of the people recommended for “an oculoplastic surgeon” were oculoplastic specialists, compared with 46.6% for “a doctor who does eyelid lifts” (Parikh et al., 2024).

Can I trust the sources an AI answer cites?

Only partly. In a peer-reviewed audit of four generative search engines, only 51.5% of generated sentences were fully supported by their citations, and only 74.5% of citations supported the sentence they were attached to (Liu, Zhang and Liang, 2023). Citations show which sources are prominent, not what caused the answer.

Can AEO guarantee that ChatGPT recommends my business?

No. No intervention studied to date guarantees a recommendation. The foundational paper on generative engine optimization found that content changes raised visibility by up to 40% on its benchmark, with effects that varied by domain. That shows visibility responds to content, not that a particular change will bring recommendations or customers to a particular business.

What is the difference between AEO and GEO?

Generative engine optimization (GEO) and answer engine optimization (AEO) describe the same goal: being cited and described correctly in AI-generated answers. GEO is the term used in academic research; AEO is more common in marketing.

How do I get my business recommended by ChatGPT, Claude or Gemini?

AI assistants name businesses whose facts they can find, read and confirm. Keep your name, location, services and prices clear and identical on your website, Google Business Profile and listings, and judge your visibility across many answers rather than one. Local AI Registry, a free AEO directory for local businesses, gives every business a free, owner-confirmed record at localairegistry.com/search as a starting point.

journal/what-is-an-ai-score/.html:
What the AI Score measures

The AI Score is a single number, from 0 to 100, that measures how findable and recommendable a local business is to AI assistants like ChatGPT, Perplexity, and Google’s AI Overviews. It is the metric we built Local AI Registry around, and we publish exactly how it is calculated. A high score means AI can find you, trust you, and name you when a customer asks; a low score means it cannot.

The number matters because the results are stark. Across the local businesses we have scored, nearly two in three land below 45 out of 100, and barely one in seventy-five clears 65. Most local businesses are not close to being recommendable by AI, and most owners have no idea where they stand.

64%of the local businesses we scored land below 45 out of 100

The AI Score exists to turn that invisible problem into one number you can see, act on, and track. It is the answer to the question every owner now has to ask: does AI recommend me, and why not?

The eight signals behind the score

The AI Score is not a black box or a single-metric gimmick. It is built from eight signals, each measuring a different part of whether an assistant can find and recommend you. Every weight is documented in our scoring methodology.

  • Retrieval grounding: can AI find and cite you for the queries that drive bookings, not just your brand name.
  • Off-property attestation: what independent sources across the web say about you.
  • AI visibility: whether specific assistants already name you today.
  • Reviews: volume, recency, rating, and whether you respond to them.
  • Google Business Profile: how complete and accurate your listing is.
  • Authority: the quality of the sites that link to and reference you.
  • Speed and mobile: whether your site is technically eligible to be cited.
  • Content and schema: whether your pages are clear and machine-readable.
The first two signals, retrieval grounding and off-property attestation, carry the most weight, because they are what actually decide an AI recommendation. The other six are eligibility: necessary, but not sufficient.

How the number is calculated

Each signal is scored on its own, then combined into the final 0-to-100 number using a weighted geometric mean rather than a simple average. The distinction matters. A geometric mean leans on your weakest signal, so a business cannot paper over a missing off-property presence with a fast website. If any load-bearing signal is near zero, the overall score stays low, which mirrors how an assistant actually behaves: one strong attribute does not earn a recommendation when a critical one is absent.

The weights come from how much each signal moves a real AI recommendation, not from what is easiest to measure. That is why two businesses with identical websites can score very differently: the one the wider web corroborates scores higher, because corroboration is what the assistant grounds its answer in.

What a good AI Score looks like

Because most local businesses score low, the bar to stand out is lower than it looks. Roughly:

  • A score of 65 or above is good: AI can reliably find and recommend you. Very few businesses are here yet.
  • A score in the 45 to 64 range is fair: you are eligible and sometimes named, with clear gaps to close.
  • Below 45 is poor: AI struggles to find or trust you, and a competitor is getting the recommendation instead.

The point of the number is not the grade, it is the diagnosis. Your AI Score comes with the specific signals dragging it down, so you know what to fix first.

Why the score is independent

No business can buy a higher AI Score, and no one can pay to be removed from a competitor’s comparison. We never sell rank, and we publish the method so anyone can check our work. That independence is the whole point: a score you could buy would tell an assistant nothing, and it would tell you nothing either.

Common questions

What is a good AI Score?

Broadly, 65 or above is good, 45 to 64 is fair, and below 45 is poor. Because most local businesses currently score below 45, even reaching the fair range puts you ahead of the majority of your competitors.

Is checking my AI Score free?

Yes. You can look up any business and see its AI Score for nothing, and registering your own business to see the full breakdown is free too.

How is an AI Score different from a Google ranking?

A Google ranking is your position in a list of blue links. An AI Score measures whether an assistant will name you at all when it answers a question with a single recommendation instead of a list. The signals overlap, but the outcome an AI Score predicts is being the answer, not being on page one.

Can I improve my AI Score?

Yes, and the score tells you how. It surfaces which of the eight signals are weakest, so you fix the ones that move an AI recommendation first, chiefly retrieval grounding and off-property attestation.

How often is the AI Score updated?

It reflects the most recent measurement of what assistants say and the underlying signals. As you improve a signal, or as the assistants change, the score is recalculated so it stays a current read rather than a one-time snapshot.
